desc:
The strings a and b have the same length and describe letter equivalences: for every index i, the letters a[i] and b[i] are equivalent. Equivalence is reflexive (a letter is equivalent to itself), symmetric and transitive: if x ~ y and y ~ z then x ~ z.

Replace every letter of base with the alphabetically smallest letter that is equivalent to it, and return the resulting string.

a = "parker", b = "morris", base = "parser"   -> "makkek"   (p~m, a~o, r~k~s, e~i)
a = "abc",    b = "cde",    base = "eed"      -> "aab"      (a~c~e, b~d)
a = "a",      b = "a",      base = "zzz"      -> "zzz"
constraints: All three strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: Letters that are linked through chains of equivalences form groups. The answer for a letter only depends on its group.
You only have 26 letters, so you can keep one representative per group. Which letter should be the representative?
Use union-find on the 26 letters. When merging two groups always make the alphabetically smaller root the parent, so that find(c) directly returns the smallest letter of the group.
editorial: Model the 26 letters as a union-find structure. For each index i, union a[i] with b[i]. If the union always attaches the root with the larger letter below the root with the smaller letter, then the root of every group is its smallest member, and find(c) gives exactly the smallest equivalent letter of c.
Finally map every character of base through find. The work is O(n α(26) + |base|). A DFS over a 26-node graph works as well; the point is that transitivity makes this a connected-components problem.
